0-rtt resumption.definition: A QUIC feature that lets a returning client send its first request alongside the handshake, so a repeat connection spends no round trip on setup.
0-rtt resumption.section_title: Three answers to TCP's mid-life crisis.

a-machine.definition: Turing's own name for his imaginary device (short for automatic machine), now called a Turing machine: a tape, a read/write head and a finite table of rules.
a-machine.section_title: Why does any of this exist?

acid.definition: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the four guarantees every relational database makes about its transactions, made precise by Jim Gray.
acid.section_title: The four properties that make money safe to move.

acquire.definition: The memory ordering a thread puts on an atomic load: everything the matching release made visible is guaranteed to be seen before any later load runs.
acquire.section_title: Concurrency without locks · the deeper rabbit hole.

addroundkey.definition: The AES round step that XORs the 128-bit state with a round key derived from the master key.
addroundkey.section_title: One key for both sides · the bulk-data workhorse.

adleman.definition: Leonard Adleman, who with Ron Rivest and Adi Shamir at MIT published RSA in 1977, the first practical public-key system.
adleman.section_title: Two strangers · a public channel · a shared secret nobody else can compute.

aes.definition: The Advanced Encryption Standard: the symmetric block cipher, Rijndael by Vincent Rijmen and Joan Daemen, chosen by NIST in 2001, that does the bulk encryption in nearly every modern system.
aes.section_title: One key for both sides · the bulk-data workhorse.

aimd.definition: Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease: TCP's rule of growing the window by one segment per round trip and halving it on loss, which Chiu and Jain proved converges to fair shares.
aimd.section_title: How fast is too fast? Ask the network.

amdahl s law.definition: Gene Amdahl's 1967 rule that if a fraction p of a program parallelises, the sequential rest caps speedup at 1/(1 − p), however many cores are added.
amdahl s law.section_title: The mathematics of how much speedup more cores can possibly give you.

ap systems.definition: Distributed stores that choose availability during a partition, serving writes on both sides and reconciling the disagreement when it heals, as Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak do.
ap systems.section_title: Pick two · the unavoidable trade in distributed storage.

arm pointer authentication.definition: A hardware defence, shipped in Apple A12 (2018) and every Apple Silicon Mac since, that cryptographically signs each return address and checks the signature when the function returns.
arm pointer authentication.section_title: Forty years of writing past the buffer · and the defenders who keep up.

arm64.definition: The 64-bit form of the ARM instruction set, which packs every instruction into a fixed 32-bit word with carefully laid-out fields.

arp.definition: Address Resolution Protocol: the local-link protocol that finds the MAC address behind an IP address by broadcasting "who has this IP?" and caching the owner's reply.

arp spoofing.definition: An attack in which a machine on the local link sends forged ARP replies claiming another host's IP address, possible because ARP has no authentication.

arpanet.definition: The ARPA-funded packet-switched network whose first message, "LO", went from UCLA to SRI in October 1969; four nodes by December, it switched to TCP/IP in 1983.
arpanet.section_title: Four nodes. A Cold War. The internet's first heartbeat.

aslr.definition: Address Space Layout Randomization: the defence that loads code, libraries, the heap and the stack at random addresses on every launch, so an attacker no longer knows where to aim.
aslr.section_title: The arms race the OS fought back

asymmetric encryption.definition: Public-key encryption: data encrypted with someone's public key opens only with their matching private key, which solves key distribution but is too slow for bulk data.
asymmetric encryption.section_title: The mathematics that makes the rest of the chapter possible.

async await.definition: JavaScript syntax (ES2017) that lets asynchronous code be written as if it were synchronous, while the compiler turns it into a Promise chain underneath.
async await.section_title: One thread. Never blocking. Forever in motion.

atomic.definition: Indivisible: describes an operation that completes as one step no other thread can see half-done, unlike counter++, which is really a read, an add and a write.
atomic.section_title: Two threads · one variable · everything depends on luck.

atomicity.definition: The ACID guarantee that a transaction either commits all of its operations or none of them.
atomicity.section_title: The four properties that make money safe to move.

attack surface.definition: Every place where an attacker can reach into a system; Stuxnet and SolarWinds showed that it includes code-signing keys and every dependency a vendor ships.
attack surface.section_title: The application layer · where the trust boundary is most often confused.

authoritative server.definition: The DNS server that holds the real answer for its own piece of the name space, such as example.com, and sets how long resolvers may cache it.
authoritative server.section_title: The phone book of the internet.

autonomous system.definition: One of the tens of thousands of independently run networks that make up the internet, each with its own number (Google is AS 15169), announcing its routes by BGP.

availability.definition: In the CAP theorem, the property that every request gets a response; a consistent system gives it up on the wrong side of a partition.
availability.section_title: Pick two · the unavoidable trade in distributed storage.

avalanche effect.definition: The property of a cryptographic hash that a single-bit change in the input produces a completely different output, with no predictable relationship to the original.
avalanche effect.section_title: The mathematics that makes the rest of the chapter possible.

b-tree.definition: A balanced, shallow search tree holding one disk page of keys per node, invented by Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight in 1970; the default index of relational databases.
b-tree.section_title: The data structure that turns O(N) into O(log N).

balanced ternary.definition: A number system with digits −1, 0 and +1, used by the Soviet Setun computer (1958); it lost to binary because three voltage levels leave narrower margins for noise.
balanced ternary.section_title: Why a computer can only count to two

bandwidth-delay product.definition: Bandwidth times round-trip time: the amount of in-flight data that fills a network path exactly without overflowing its buffers, and the level BBR tries to hold its window at.
bandwidth-delay product.section_title: Three answers to TCP's mid-life crisis.

baran.definition: Paul Baran of the RAND Corporation, who between 1960 and 1964 argued for a survivable mesh network with no centre, its messages broken into independently routed blocks.

base.definition: The control terminal of a transistor (the gate, in the modern field-effect design): a small voltage here lets a much larger current flow between collector and emitter.

bbr.definition: Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time: Google's 2016 congestion control, which ignores loss as a signal and instead measures bandwidth and RTT to aim for the bandwidth-delay product.
bbr.section_title: Three answers to TCP's mid-life crisis.

bcp 38.definition: The best current practice from 2000 asking every ISP to filter outgoing packets so customers cannot spoof source addresses; a quarter-century later it is still unevenly deployed.
bcp 38.section_title: Trust the source field at your peril.

bcpl.definition: Martin Richards's typeless, word-oriented language (Cambridge, 1967), designed for writing compilers; Thompson's B was a smaller BCPL, and Ritchie's C came after B.

bdp.definition: Bandwidth-delay product: bandwidth times round-trip time, the amount of in-flight data that fills a network path exactly without overflowing its buffers.
bdp.section_title: Three answers to TCP's mid-life crisis.

bell labs.definition: The research laboratory where Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie built UNIX from 1969 and C in 1972, and where Bjarne Stroustrup began C++ in 1979.
bell labs.section_label: 02 · Ritchie and Thompson at Bell Labs
bell labs.section_title: Two men, a discarded minicomputer, four years.

berners-lee.definition: Tim Berners-Lee, the British physicist at CERN who proposed the World Wide Web in 1989, defined URL, HTTP and HTML, and wrote the first web server and browser.
berners-lee.section_title: A proposal that nobody asked for.

bernstein.definition: Daniel J. Bernstein, who in 1996 invented SYN cookies, the defence that lets a server survive a SYN flood without keeping per-connection state.
bernstein.section_label: 06 · SYN floods, cookies, and the rest

bgp.definition: Border Gateway Protocol: the protocol, born in 1989, by which the internet's independent networks tell each other which address prefixes they can reach, trusting whatever their peers say.

bgp hijacking.definition: An attack, or accident, in which an autonomous system announces routes for IP prefixes it does not own and pulls their traffic, as Pakistan Telecom did to YouTube in 2008.
bgp hijacking.section_title: Where the network can lie · and where TLS prevents it from mattering.

bit.definition: Short for binary digit: the smallest unit of information, a single 0 or 1, as held by a wire that is either on or off.
bit.section_title: Why a computer can only count to two

bitcoin mining.definition: The brute-force search for a block whose SHA-256 hash starts with a required number of leading zeros; that difficulty regulates the supply of new coins.
bitcoin mining.section_title: The fingerprint that does not let you reconstruct the face.

black hat.definition: The enterprise-oriented security conference held in the same week as DEF CON.
black hat.section_label: 06 · The culture · the ecosystem of breaking and fixing
black hat.section_title: The unified theory · and the people who keep the system honest.

body.definition: The optional part of an HTTP request or response after the blank line that ends the headers: the document returned, or the data a POST or PUT sends.

bombe.definition: The electromechanical machine Turing built at Bletchley Park to break Enigma, racing through candidate rotor positions and discarding any that led to a contradiction.
bombe.section_title: Why does any of this exist?

boole.definition: George Boole (1815–1864), the self-taught English mathematician whose The Mathematical Analysis of Logic (1847) recast logic as an algebra whose variables are true or false.
boole.section_title: The Victorian schoolteacher who reduced logic to algebra

boolean algebra.definition: George Boole's algebra of true and false (AND, OR, NOT), published in 1847, which Shannon in 1937 showed relay circuits can compute; logic gates are its physical form.
boolean algebra.section_label: 01 · The computer as a mathematical object
boolean algebra.section_title: Every layer is math made physical · made physical again, on top.

bootloader.definition: A small program the firmware loads at power-on, whose only job is to find the kernel image on disk, load it into memory and jump to its entry point.
bootloader.section_title: The kernel is just a program

buffer overflow.definition: A bug in which a program writes more data than a buffer can hold, so the extra bytes spill into adjacent memory, such as a saved return address.

byte.definition: A group of eight bits, enough to represent 256 distinct values.
byte.section_title: Why a computer can only count to two

bytecode.definition: A sequence of small, simple opcodes for a virtual machine, into which Python compiles source code before the interpreter executes it.

c++.definition: Bjarne Stroustrup's extension of Ritchie's C, begun at Bell Labs in 1979 as C with Classes and renamed in 1983: object orientation with no runtime cost unless used.

cache coherence.definition: The property that each core's private caches still agree with one another about memory, maintained in hardware by protocols such as MESI.
cache coherence.section_label: 06 · NUMA & MESI · the modern hardware reality
cache coherence.section_title: Memory is not flat any more · cache coherence is the only reason it pretends to be.

cache line.definition: The fixed-size block, typically 64 bytes, in which caches hold memory; coherence protocols such as MESI track the state of each line on every core.
cache line.section_label: 06 · NUMA & MESI · the modern hardware reality
cache line.section_title: Memory is not flat any more · cache coherence is the only reason it pretends to be.

caches.definition: Small, fast memory built directly into the CPU that holds copies of recently used data, so most accesses avoid the long round trip to main RAM.
caches.section_title: Von Neumann's insight: instructions are data

callback.definition: A function passed to whoever does some slow work, to be called back when the work is done: JavaScript's first way of handling asynchronous I/O.
callback.section_title: One thread. Never blocking. Forever in motion.

callback pyramid of doom.definition: Code with three or four callbacks nested inside each other, indentation marching across the screen and error handling impossible: the price of JavaScript's callback era.
callback pyramid of doom.section_title: One thread. Never blocking. Forever in motion.

callbacks.definition: Functions passed to whoever does a slow piece of work, to be called back when it finishes: the first of JavaScript's three eras of asynchronous code.
callbacks.section_title: One thread. Never blocking. Forever in motion.

calling convention.definition: A contract between caller and callee about who puts arguments where, who saves which registers, and how return values are delivered, such as the System V AMD64 ABI.

cam-table overflow.definition: Another name for MAC flooding: filling a switch's MAC table with fabricated source addresses until it falls back to broadcasting every frame to every port, like a hub.

cap theorem.definition: Eric Brewer's result (conjectured 2000, proven 2002 by Gilbert and Lynch) that a distributed data store can provide at most two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance.
cap theorem.section_title: Pick two · the unavoidable trade in distributed storage.

capital one 2019 breach.definition: The breach in which a former AWS engineer used SSRF against Capital One's web application firewall to fetch cloud credentials and exfiltrate 100 million customer records.
capital one 2019 breach.section_title: The application layer · where the trust boundary is most often confused.

capture the flag.definition: A security contest in which participants find and exploit flaws in deliberately broken software and submit hidden strings, the flags, as proof; the field's training ground.
capture the flag.section_label: 06 · The culture · the ecosystem of breaking and fixing
capture the flag.section_title: The unified theory · and the people who keep the system honest.

carrier wave.definition: A high-frequency sinusoid that a medium such as radio, DSL or cable can transport, onto which bits are imposed by modulation.
carrier wave.section_title: How a one-or-zero rides on a continuous wave.

cbc.definition: Cipher Block Chaining: a block-cipher mode that XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, so identical plaintext blocks encrypt differently.
cbc.section_title: One key for both sides · the bulk-data workhorse.

ccc.definition: Chaos Communication Congress: the European centre of the hacker conference circuit, held in Hamburg in late December.
ccc.section_label: 06 · The culture · the ecosystem of breaking and fixing
ccc.section_title: The unified theory · and the people who keep the system honest.

cerf.definition: Vint Cerf, who with Bob Kahn published the 1974 paper that defined TCP/IP, the protocols ARPANET switched to in 1983.

cern.definition: The European particle physics laboratory outside Geneva where Tim Berners-Lee proposed and built the World Wide Web, released into the public domain in 1993.
cern.section_title: A proposal that nobody asked for.

certificate authority.definition: An organisation trusted to sign certificates, vouching that a public key belongs to the hostnames named; its own certificate is signed by a more trusted one, up to a root.
certificate authority.section_title: One round trip · two strangers · a perfect channel.

certificate transparency.definition: The system (RFC 6962, 2013; mandatory in Chrome since 2018) that logs every certificate a CA issues in a public, append-only Merkle-tree log that domain owners can monitor.
certificate transparency.section_label: 06 · Putting it together · TLS at depth · post-quantum
certificate transparency.section_title: Where every primitive lands · and what threatens them.

cet.definition: Control-flow Enforcement Technology: Intel's hardware defence, centred on a shadow stack, against ROP and JOP; it has shipped in 11th-generation Core CPUs since 2020.
cet.section_title: Forty years of writing past the buffer · and the defenders who keep up.

cfi.definition: Control-Flow Integrity: a compiler-inserted runtime check that every indirect call or return lands on a target the compiler judged valid for that call site.
cfi.section_title: Forty years of writing past the buffer · and the defenders who keep up.

cfs.definition: Completely Fair Scheduler: Linux's default scheduler from 2007 to 2023, which keeps runnable processes in a red-black tree by virtual runtime and always runs the one with the least.

cgnat.definition: Carrier-Grade NAT: an ISP sharing one public IPv4 address among hundreds or thousands of customers behind a translation layer, the stopgap after IPv4 addresses ran out.
cgnat.section_title: The thirty-year migration that still isn't done.

cgroup.definition: Control group: a Linux kernel feature that limits how much CPU time, memory, disk I/O and network bandwidth a group of processes may use.

channel capacity.definition: The highest bit rate a channel can carry reliably, C = B · log₂(1 + SNR): below it errors can be made arbitrarily rare, above it they are inevitable.
channel capacity.section_title: 1948. Bell Labs again. The number behind every wire.

cipher suite.definition: A named combination of cryptographic algorithms for a TLS connection; the client's hello lists the suites it supports.
cipher suite.section_title: One round trip · two strangers · a perfect channel.

circuit switching.definition: The telephone network's model: reserving a dedicated end-to-end path between two parties for the whole call, whether or not anyone is speaking.

cisc.definition: Complex Instruction Set Computer: a design, like x86, with many specialised instructions, including multi-step operations such as load, add and store back in a single instruction.

closure.definition: The property of relational algebra that every operation returns a relation, so any result can feed the next operation; it is what makes SQL composable.
closure.section_title: The math under SQL · three operators do most of the work.

codasyl.definition: The network-model database standard drawn up by committee in 1969, which stored data as a graph that programs navigated by following pointers.
codasyl.section_title: One paper. One change of model. Fifty years of consequence.

codd.definition: Edgar F. Codd, the IBM researcher whose 1970 paper on a relational model of data founded relational databases; he won the ACM Turing Award in 1981.
codd.section_title: One paper. One change of model. Fifty years of consequence.

collector.definition: One of a transistor's two current-carrying terminals (the drain, in the field-effect design); current flows from collector to emitter while the base carries a voltage.

collision resistance.definition: The hash property that no practical algorithm finds any two distinct inputs with the same hash; the weakest of the three, and the first to fail.
collision resistance.section_title: The fingerprint that does not let you reconstruct the face.

colossus.definition: The first programmable electronic digital computer, built by Tommy Flowers to break the Lorenz cipher used by Hitler's high command.
colossus.section_title: Why does any of this exist?

compare-and-swap.definition: The atomic instruction (CAS) that changes a value from x to y only if it is still x, as one indivisible step; the foundation of mutexes and lock-free structures.
compare-and-swap.section_title: Concurrency without locks · the deeper rabbit hole.

compiler.definition: A program that translates source code into a lower-level form: machine code for C, or, inside CPython, bytecode for a stack-based virtual machine.
compiler.section_title: CPython is one million lines of C running your script.

computer emergency response team.definition: CERT, founded at Carnegie Mellon with DARPA funding within weeks of the 1988 Morris worm: the first organisation tasked with coordinating response to internet security incidents.
computer emergency response team.section_title: Trust the source field at your peril.

confusion.definition: The cipher property that each output bit depends in a complicated way on the key; in AES the non-linear SubBytes step supplies it.
confusion.section_title: One key for both sides · the bulk-data workhorse.

congestion avoidance.definition: TCP's phase after a loss: the congestion window is halved, then grows linearly by one segment per round trip until the next loss.
congestion avoidance.section_title: How fast is too fast? Ask the network.

congestion avoidance and control.definition: Van Jacobson and Michael Karels's 1988 paper diagnosing the 1986 congestion collapse, whose fix (slow start and AIMD) became part of every TCP stack.
congestion avoidance and control.section_title: How fast is too fast? Ask the network.

congestion control.definition: The machinery that keeps a TCP sender from outrunning the network in between, as flow control keeps it from outrunning the receiver.
congestion control.section_title: How fast is too fast? Ask the network.

connection migration.definition: A QUIC feature: the connection ID lives at the application level, so a phone switching from Wi-Fi to cellular keeps its connection, which TCP, tied to addresses and ports, cannot.
connection migration.section_title: Three answers to TCP's mid-life crisis.

consensus.definition: The formal problem of getting n machines to agree on a value despite up to f of them failing; Paxos and Raft are its classic protocols.
consensus.section_title: Many machines · agreement · the math says it shouldn't quite work · we make it work anyway.

consistency.definition: The ACID guarantee that a transaction beginning in a valid database state ends in one, with referential integrity, constraints and data types intact.
consistency.section_title: The four properties that make money safe to move.

container.definition: An isolated process built from kernel namespaces and cgroups that shares the host's kernel, so it starts in milliseconds and weighs a few megabytes.
container.section_title: Lighter than VMs · faster to start · the deployment unit of the modern web.

container runtime.definition: The software on a Kubernetes worker node that actually runs the pods' containers, such as containerd or CRI-O.
container runtime.section_title: The orchestrator that took over deployment.

content security policy.definition: A response header in which the server lists the origins the browser may load scripts and other resources from, so injected scripts are refused even when an XSS injection succeeds.
content security policy.section_title: Four boundaries that keep the web from being one big shared computer.

control flow integrity.definition: A defence against return-oriented programming in which the compiler records where indirect jumps may legally land and the runtime refuses any transfer to an address off that list.
control flow integrity.section_title: The arms race the OS fought back

control loop.definition: The idea at the heart of Kubernetes: the user declares how the system should look, and controllers continuously observe how it does look and reconcile the difference.
control loop.section_title: The orchestrator that took over deployment.

control plane.definition: The coordinating layer of a system: in Kubernetes the API server, etcd, scheduler and controller manager; in a service mesh, the hub that pushes rules and certificates to sidecars.
control plane.section_title: Architecture is fashion · the same problems return every fifteen years.

control theory.definition: The mathematics of feedback: observe a system, compare it with a target, correct, repeat; the shape behind TCP congestion control and Kubernetes' reconcile loop.
control theory.section_title: The orchestrator that took over deployment.

control-flow integrity.definition: A defence, proposed by Martín Abadi and colleagues in 2005, that checks at run time that every indirect call or return targets an address the compiler judged valid.
control-flow integrity.section_title: Forty years of writing past the buffer · and the defenders who keep up.

cookie.definition: In a SYN cookie, the keyed hash of a connection's addresses, ports and a time bucket that a flooded server returns as its Initial Sequence Number, storing nothing.
cookie.section_label: 06 · SYN floods, cookies, and the rest

cooperative.definition: Of multitasking: each running program voluntarily yields the CPU back to the scheduler, so one program that never yields freezes the whole machine.

copy-on-write.definition: Sharing data read-only and making a private copy only when something writes to it: how fork() avoids duplicating memory, and how ZFS, btrfs and APFS never overwrite blocks.
copy-on-write.section_title: A tree of names on a flat array of blocks

cors.definition: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: an opt-in escape hatch from the same-origin policy, in which a server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers to let other origins read its responses.
cors.section_title: Four boundaries that keep the web from being one big shared computer.

cow.definition: Copy-on-write: sharing pages or blocks read-only and making a private copy only at the moment one side writes.

cp systems.definition: Distributed stores that choose consistency during a partition, refusing writes rather than risk disagreement, as etcd, ZooKeeper and Google Spanner do.
cp systems.section_title: Pick two · the unavoidable trade in distributed storage.

cross-site request forgery.definition: An attack in which a page on another site makes the victim's browser send a request, such as a bank transfer, that automatically carries the target site's session cookie.
cross-site request forgery.section_title: Four boundaries that keep the web from being one big shared computer.

cross-site scripting.definition: An attack that injects the attacker's script into a site's own pages, so it runs with that origin's full privileges; for two decades the most common web vulnerability.
cross-site scripting.section_title: Four boundaries that keep the web from being one big shared computer.

csma cd.definition: Carrier Sense, Multiple Access with Collision Detection, Ethernet's shared-cable rule: listen before sending, and if two signals collide, both back off for a random interval and retry.

csp.definition: Content Security Policy: a response header listing the origins the browser may load scripts and other resources from, so injected scripts are refused.
csp.section_title: Four boundaries that keep the web from being one big shared computer.

csrf.definition: Cross-site request forgery: a page on another site makes the victim's browser send a request that automatically carries the target site's session cookie.
csrf.section_title: Four boundaries that keep the web from being one big shared computer.

csrf token.definition: A random, unguessable token a server puts in a hidden form field and requires back with every submission, which a forging site cannot read.
csrf token.section_title: Four boundaries that keep the web from being one big shared computer.

ctf.definition: Capture The Flag: a contest in which participants exploit deliberately broken software and submit hidden flags as proof; the training ground for security engineers.
ctf.section_label: 06 · The culture · the ecosystem of breaking and fixing
ctf.section_title: The unified theory · and the people who keep the system honest.

ctr.definition: Counter Mode: a block-cipher mode that turns AES into a stream cipher by encrypting an incrementing counter and XORing the result with the plaintext.
ctr.section_title: One key for both sides · the bulk-data workhorse.

cubic.definition: Linux's default TCP congestion control since 2006: still loss-based, but its window grows as a cubic function, easing near the size that last caused loss, then probing past it.
cubic.section_title: Three answers to TCP's mid-life crisis.

cuda.definition: NVIDIA's programming model, introduced around 2007, that opens the GPU to general parallel computation through a hierarchy of threads, warps, blocks and grids.
cuda.section_title: The other shape of parallelism · thousands of small cores doing the same thing.

data model.definition: A definition of the shape data takes; Codd's relational one admits only rows in tables, with no pointers, hierarchies or embedded references.
data model.section_title: One paper. One change of model. Fifty years of consequence.

data-as-code.definition: The attack pattern in which bytes a developer believed inert are parsed and executed as instructions, as in SQL injection, XSS, deserialisation attacks and prompt injection.
data-as-code.section_title: The application layer · where the trust boundary is most often confused.

ddl.definition: Data Definition Language: the half of SQL that changes the schema, with statements such as CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and CREATE INDEX.
ddl.section_title: Declarative · standardised · still arguing about itself.

def con.definition: The largest hacker conference in the world, held every August in Las Vegas.
def con.section_label: 06 · The culture · the ecosystem of breaking and fixing
def con.section_title: The unified theory · and the people who keep the system honest.

defence in depth.definition: The discipline of stacking independent defensive layers and designing each as if it were the last, on the assumption that any other layer might be bypassed.
defence in depth.section_title: The application layer · where the trust boundary is most often confused.

dep.definition: Data Execution Prevention: Windows's name for marking writable memory as non-executable, so bytes smuggled into a buffer cannot run as instructions; Linux calls it the NX bit.

determinism.definition: The property of a hash function that the same input always produces the same hash.
determinism.section_title: The mathematics that makes the rest of the chapter possible.

diffie.definition: Whitfield Diffie, who with Martin Hellman published "New Directions in Cryptography" in 1976, showing how two strangers can agree on a secret in public; both won the 2015 Turing Award.
diffie.section_title: Three ideas before the algorithms · so the rest of the chapter is grounded.

diffie hellman.definition: The 1976 key-exchange protocol by which two strangers agree on a shared secret over a public channel; its security rests on the hardness of the discrete logarithm.
diffie hellman.section_title: Three ideas before the algorithms · so the rest of the chapter is grounded.

diffusion.definition: The cipher property that each input bit influences every output bit; in AES, ShiftRows and MixColumns spread it across the state.
diffusion.section_title: One key for both sides · the bulk-data workhorse.

direct memory access.definition: The channel by which a device, once told where to read and write, copies data into or out of RAM on its own, without the CPU handling every byte.
direct memory access.section_title: How the CPU reaches beyond itself

dirty cow.definition: A Linux bug (CVE-2016-5195), in the kernel since 2007 and found in 2016: a race in copy-on-write handling that let an unprivileged process write to read-only files.

dirtypipe.definition: A 2022 Linux privilege-escalation bug: a flaw in pipe-buffer initialisation that allowed writes to read-only files.

dma.definition: Direct memory access: a device copying data into or out of RAM on its own, without the CPU touching each byte, then raising an interrupt when it is done.
dma.section_title: How the CPU reaches beyond itself

dml.definition: Data Manipulation Language: the half of SQL that reads and changes the data, through SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.
dml.section_title: Declarative · standardised · still arguing about itself.

dns.definition: Domain Name System: the hierarchical, replicated, cached distributed database, designed by Paul Mockapetris in 1983, that translates names like example.com into IP addresses.
dns.section_title: The phone book of the internet.

dns poisoning.definition: An attack that tricks a recursive resolver into caching a forged answer, which it then serves to every user behind it; Dan Kaminsky made it practical in 2008.
dns poisoning.section_title: Where the network can lie · and where TLS prevents it from mattering.

docker.definition: The container tool, released in 2013, that gave containers a usable interface and a portable image format built from layers.
docker.section_title: Lighter than VMs · faster to start · the deployment unit of the modern web.

dom.definition: Document Object Model: the tree of objects a browser parses HTML into, which JavaScript reads and changes through methods like document.querySelector().
dom.section_title: From bytes to pixels in five steps.

dom-based xss.definition: Cross-site scripting carried out entirely in the browser, by page JavaScript that writes URL parameters into the DOM unsafely.
dom-based xss.section_title: Four boundaries that keep the web from being one big shared computer.

domain name system.definition: The hierarchical, replicated, cached, mostly decentralised database, designed by Paul Mockapetris in 1983, that translates human-readable names into IP addresses.
domain name system.section_title: The phone book of the internet.

doping.definition: Salting pure silicon with a trace of another element, whose spare electrons or vacancies (holes) give the crystal mobile carriers, so a small voltage can switch it.

dpl.definition: Descriptor Privilege Level: the field in each interrupt descriptor table entry that controls whether user code may raise that vector by software.
dpl.section_title: The one door between the two worlds

durability.definition: The ACID guarantee that once a transaction is reported committed, its data survives any later crash, power loss or hardware failure short of total disk loss.
durability.section_title: The four properties that make money safe to move.

dyn.definition: A major DNS provider, host of authoritative servers for Twitter, GitHub and others, whose flooding by the Mirai botnet on 21 October 2016 made those sites unreachable for hours.
dyn.section_title: The phone book of the internet.

ebpf.definition: Extended Berkeley Packet Filter: a Linux feature that lets user programs load small pieces of code into the running kernel, checked by a verifier and run in Ring 0.

ecb.definition: Electronic Codebook: the simplest block-cipher mode, encrypting each block independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks show up as identical ciphertext blocks.
ecb.section_title: One key for both sides · the bulk-data workhorse.

ecc.definition: Elliptic curve cryptography: public-key cryptography built on the discrete logarithm over points of an elliptic curve, where a 256-bit key matches 3072-bit RSA.
ecc.section_title: Same trapdoor · curves instead of integers · much smaller keys.

ecdh.definition: Elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman: the Diffie–Hellman key exchange run on elliptic-curve points instead of integers modulo a prime; the key exchange of choice in TLS 1.3.
ecdh.section_label: 06 · Putting it together · TLS at depth · post-quantum
ecdh.section_title: Where every primitive lands · and what threatens them.

ecdsa.definition: The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm: an elliptic-curve signature scheme used by TLS 1.3, alongside Ed25519, and by Bitcoin.
ecdsa.section_label: 06 · Putting it together · TLS at depth · post-quantum
ecdsa.section_title: Where every primitive lands · and what threatens them.

ed25519.definition: The elliptic-curve signature scheme published in 2011 by Daniel J. Bernstein and collaborators, used by TLS 1.3, SSH, Signal and WireGuard.
ed25519.section_title: Same trapdoor · curves instead of integers · much smaller keys.

edr.definition: Endpoint detection and response: agents on every laptop and server that model normal process behaviour and alert on anomalies; the defence generation of the mid-2010s.
edr.section_title: From firewalls to zero trust · five generations of how to defend a network.

eevdf.definition: Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First: Linux's default scheduler since kernel 6.6 (2023), keeping CFS's virtual-runtime bookkeeping but giving every task an explicit deadline.

eich.definition: Brendan Eich, the Netscape engineer who in May 1995 had ten working days to design the language that became JavaScript, first called Mocha, then LiveScript.
eich.section_title: Ten days. Three names. One language.

elliptic curve.definition: The set of points satisfying an equation of the form y² = x³ + ax + b; over a finite field its points form a group, the basis of ECC.
elliptic curve.section_title: Same trapdoor · curves instead of integers · much smaller keys.

emitter.definition: One of a transistor's two current-carrying terminals (the source, in the field-effect design); a voltage at the base lets current flow between collector and emitter.

etcd.definition: The distributed key-value store, kept consistent by Raft, that is Kubernetes' source of truth: every desired-state object lives there.
etcd.section_title: The orchestrator that took over deployment.

ethernet.definition: The local-area network Bob Metcalfe invented at Xerox PARC in 1973: computers sharing one cable under CSMA/CD, today switched, but still framed with 48-bit MAC addresses.

evaluator.definition: CPython's bytecode loop (ceval.c): a giant switch statement that reads each bytecode and dispatches it to the C handler that carries it out.
evaluator.section_title: CPython is one million lines of C running your script.

event loop.definition: The mechanism that runs JavaScript on one never-blocking thread: take one task from the macrotask queue, run it to completion, drain the microtask queue, perhaps render, repeat.
event loop.section_title: One thread. Never blocking. Forever in motion.

eventual consistency.definition: The trade Dynamo-style stores make: keep serving, possibly with stale reads, and let replicas disagree for a while before reconciling, rather than insist every node agrees now.
eventual consistency.section_title: Many machines · agreement · the math says it shouldn't quite work · we make it work anyway.

everything is a file.definition: The UNIX creed that the keyboard, the network connection and the running process are all reached through the same few calls as ordinary files.
everything is a file.section_title: Why the kernel had to be invented

false sharing.definition: A slowdown in which two unrelated variables share one 64-byte cache line, so writes from different cores make the line ping-pong between their caches.
false sharing.section_label: 06 · NUMA & MESI · the modern hardware reality
false sharing.section_title: Memory is not flat any more · cache coherence is the only reason it pretends to be.

firewall.definition: A filter at the network perimeter that decides which traffic may cross; from the 1990s, the first of the five generations of network defence.
firewall.section_title: From firewalls to zero trust · five generations of how to defend a network.

flp impossibility result.definition: Fischer, Lynch and Paterson's 1985 proof that in an asynchronous system where even one process can crash, no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee both safety and liveness.
flp impossibility result.section_title: Many machines · agreement · the math says it shouldn't quite work · we make it work anyway.

forensics.definition: The security discipline, and CTF category, of finding evidence in a memory dump, network capture or filesystem image.
forensics.section_label: 06 · The culture · the ecosystem of breaking and fixing
forensics.section_title: The unified theory · and the people who keep the system honest.

fork.definition: The UNIX system call that creates a child process as a copy of its parent's address space, made nearly free by copy-on-write.

forward secrecy.definition: The guarantee that recorded encrypted traffic stays unreadable even if the server's long-term private key is stolen later, because each session key came from ephemeral keys since discarded.
forward secrecy.section_title: One round trip · two strangers · a perfect channel.

fragmented.definition: Of a heap: broken by repeated allocations and frees into many small free chunks, none large enough for the next big request, though total free space may be huge.
fragmented.section_title: You allocated it. You free it.

fragments.definition: The pieces of an IP packet too large for a link's MTU, each a complete IP packet sharing the original's Identification field, with its own Fragment Offset.

full adder.definition: A circuit that adds three input bits (A, B and a carry-in) to give a sum bit and a carry-out, built from two half adders and an OR gate.
full adder.section_title: How a circuit learns to add

gadget.definition: In return-oriented programming, a short snippet of existing code, one or two instructions ending in ret, that the attacker chains with others to build arbitrary computation.
gadget.section_title: The arms race the OS fought back

gcm.definition: Galois Counter Mode: CTR-mode encryption plus an authentication tag, giving confidentiality and integrity in one operation; the modern recommended block-cipher mode.
gcm.section_title: One key for both sides · the bulk-data workhorse.

gil.definition: Global Interpreter Lock: the single lock in CPython that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so reference counts cannot race.
gil.section_title: One Python thread runs at a time. There are reasons. They are running out.

git commit ids.definition: The hashes that name Git commits, each covering its parent's hash, the file contents and the author and message, so tampering with history changes every later ID.
git commit ids.section_title: The fingerprint that does not let you reconstruct the face.

graph theory.definition: The mathematics of nodes joined by edges, beneath the routing of Chapter 9 and the wait-for graph of deadlock; one of the primitives that outlast every substrate.
graph theory.section_title: The substrate is changing again · which parts will survive it?

gustafson s law.definition: The 1988 counterpart to Amdahl's law: when the problem grows with the machine, the parallel part scales while the sequential part stays roughly constant, so speedup grows nearly linearly.
gustafson s law.section_title: The mathematics of how much speedup more cores can possibly give you.

half adder.definition: A circuit that adds two single bits: an XOR gives the sum and an AND gives the carry, both sharing the same two inputs.
half adder.section_title: How a circuit learns to add

hard link.definition: A directory entry pointing to an inode; one file can have several, each a name for it, and the file is deleted only when its link count drops to zero.
hard link.section_title: A tree of names on a flat array of blocks

hardware timer.definition: A free-running counter wired into the interrupt controller that fires interrupts at a programmed rate, letting the kernel take the CPU back and making preemptive multitasking possible.
hardware timer.section_title: The piece of silicon that makes multitasking possible

hash function.definition: A one-way function turning data of any size into a fixed-length fingerprint (256 bits for SHA-256): deterministic, infeasible to invert, and scrambled completely by any one-bit change.
hash function.section_title: The mathematics that makes the rest of the chapter possible.

headers.definition: The name-colon-value lines that follow an HTTP request line or status line, one per line, ended by a blank line.

heap.definition: The region of memory for long-lived allocations, requested explicitly (malloc in C) and managed by an allocator, unlike the self-managing stack.
heap.section_title: You allocated it. You free it.

hellman.definition: Martin Hellman, who with Whitfield Diffie published Diffie–Hellman key agreement in 1976, letting two strangers agree on a shared secret over a public channel.
hellman.section_title: The mathematics that makes the rest of the chapter possible.

hmac.definition: Hash-based message authentication code: a keyed hash that proves a message is intact and authentic; TLS 1.3 derives its session keys through HKDF, which is built on it.
hmac.section_label: 06 · Putting it together · TLS at depth · post-quantum
hmac.section_title: Where every primitive lands · and what threatens them.

horizontal escalation.definition: A privilege escalation that moves sideways, at the same privilege level, into another process's or user's data.

html.definition: HyperText Markup Language: Berners-Lee's simple text format for documents, with links to other documents written inline rather than as appendices.
html.section_title: A proposal that nobody asked for.

http.definition: HyperText Transfer Protocol: the stateless request-and-response protocol by which one machine asks another for the document at a URL and receives it back.

http 2.definition: The 2015 version of HTTP (RFC 7540, derived from Google's SPDY) that replaced the text wire format with binary frames, multiplexing many streams over one TCP connection.
http 2.section_title: The two upgrades that broke compatibility on purpose.

http 3.definition: HTTP semantics carried over QUIC instead of TCP (RFC 9114, 2022), so a lost packet stalls only its own stream rather than every request on the connection.
http 3.section_title: The two upgrades that broke compatibility on purpose.

https.definition: HTTP run over TLS, so every byte between browser and server is encrypted and the server's identity is proven by its certificate.
https.section_title: One round trip · two strangers · a perfect channel.

hypervisor.definition: The layer that runs virtual machines, intercepting the guests' privileged operations; type 1 sits directly on the hardware, type 2 runs inside a host operating system.
hypervisor.section_title: One physical machine · pretending to be many.

iana.definition: The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, keeper of the central pool of IPv4 addresses, which ran dry on 3 February 2011, ahead of the regional registries.
iana.section_title: The thirty-year migration that still isn't done.

icann.definition: The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers: the body that chooses the operator of each DNS top-level domain, such as VeriSign for .com, and one of the root's operators.
icann.section_title: The phone book of the internet.

icmp.definition: Internet Control Message Protocol: IP's control-message companion (protocol number 1), used for example when a router reports that a packet's TTL reached zero.

idempotency.definition: The property of a request that repeating it has the same effect as sending it once: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST typically is not.

idt.definition: Interrupt descriptor table: the table the kernel writes at boot that tells the CPU which handler to run for each exception, hardware interrupt or legacy system-call vector.
idt.section_title: The one door between the two worlds

ieee.definition: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers: the standards body behind IEEE 754 floating point, which also assigns manufacturers the OUI prefixes of their MAC addresses.
ieee.section_title: Four engineering goals, written 1974, still in force.

ieee 754.definition: The floating-point standard, published by the IEEE in 1985, that defines how processors represent fractional numbers; every JavaScript number is a 64-bit IEEE 754 double.
ieee 754.section_title: Ten days. Three names. One language.

ietf.definition: The Internet Engineering Task Force: the body whose RFCs standardise internet protocols, from QUIC in 2021 to the catalogue of BGP route-leak types in RFC 7908.
ietf.section_title: Trust the source field at your peril.

ihl.definition: Internet Header Length: the IPv4 header field giving the header's length in 4-byte units, almost always 5.

in flight.definition: Sent but not yet acknowledged: the bytes a TCP sender has transmitted and must keep in its retransmit buffer until an acknowledgement arrives.
in flight.section_title: How fast is too fast? Ask the network.

independence principle.definition: Codd's principle that queries describe the result wanted, not the procedure, leaving the engine free to choose any execution strategy that produces the same answer.
independence principle.section_title: One paper. One change of model. Fifty years of consequence.

infinity.definition: The IEEE 754 special value with an all-ones exponent and a zero mantissa, produced by dividing by zero or overflowing the largest representable number; the sign bit gives its direction.

information theory.definition: Claude Shannon's 1948 mathematics of communication, which gave information a unit (the bit) and a formula (entropy) and proved every channel has a maximum reliable bit rate.
information theory.section_title: 1948. Bell Labs again. The number behind every wire.

inheritance.definition: Building one class on another; in memory, one struct embedded inside another.

inode.definition: The UNIX filesystem structure holding everything about a file except its name and data: size, owner, permissions, timestamps, link count and the list of data blocks.
inode.section_title: A tree of names on a flat array of blocks

instruction cycle.definition: The loop every CPU core runs without pause: fetch an instruction, decode it, execute it, write back the result, then advance the program counter and start again.

instruction set architecture.definition: The menu of binary patterns a processor executes and the operation each one means: the contract between hardware and software, such as x86, ARM or RISC-V.

integrated circuit.definition: Multiple transistors etched onto a single piece of semiconductor, first made by Jack Kilby in germanium in 1958 and, within months, by Robert Noyce in silicon.

inter-process communication.definition: The controlled set of kernel mechanisms (pipes, signals, shared memory, semaphores, sockets) through which otherwise isolated processes exchange data and coordinate.

iommu.definition: A second MMU that translates and bounds-checks the addresses devices use for DMA, so a buggy or malicious device cannot write into kernel memory.
iommu.section_title: How the CPU reaches beyond itself

ip.definition: The Internet Protocol: the network layer that carries packets best-effort from any source to any destination, each led by a header that every router reads to forward it.

ip header.definition: The fixed fields opening every packet (twenty bytes in IPv4) that routers read to decide where it goes next, whether to fragment it and when to drop it.

ip spoofing.definition: Writing a false source address into a packet's IP header, possible because the source field is set by the sender and verified nowhere along the path.
ip spoofing.section_title: Trust the source field at your peril.

ipc.definition: Inter-process communication: the kernel's controlled mechanisms, such as pipes, signals, shared memory and sockets, that let isolated processes talk.

ipv4.definition: The original Internet Protocol, dating to 1981, with 32-bit addresses (about 4.3 billion) that ran out at IANA's central pool in 2011.

ipv6.definition: The successor to IPv4, defined in 1995, with 128-bit addresses; because v4-only and v6-only machines cannot talk directly, the migration is still incomplete thirty years on.
ipv6.section_title: The thirty-year migration that still isn't done.

isa.definition: Instruction set architecture: the menu of binary patterns a processor executes and what each one means, the contract between hardware and software.

isn.definition: Initial Sequence Number: the starting value of a TCP connection's sequence counter, chosen by each side in the handshake and now randomised so attackers cannot predict it.
isn.section_label: 06 · SYN floods, cookies, and the rest

jacobson.definition: Van Jacobson, the LBL researcher who with Michael Karels diagnosed the 1986 congestion collapse and, in their 1988 paper, added slow start and AIMD to TCP.
jacobson.section_title: How fast is too fast? Ask the network.

javascript.definition: The scripting language Brendan Eich designed in ten days at Netscape in 1995, first called Mocha, then LiveScript; it runs in every browser and, via Node.js, on servers.
javascript.section_title: The two upgrades that broke compatibility on purpose.

jop.definition: Jump-oriented programming: a code-reuse attack like ROP that chains existing instruction sequences through indirect jumps instead of returns.
jop.section_title: Forty years of writing past the buffer · and the defenders who keep up.

journal.definition: A small, dedicated disk region where a filesystem writes each intended change before applying it, so crash recovery replays the journal instead of scanning the disk.
journal.section_title: A tree of names on a flat array of blocks

journaling.definition: Of a filesystem: writing every change first to a journal, then to its real place, so a crash is recovered in seconds rather than hours.
journaling.section_title: A tree of names on a flat array of blocks

kahn.definition: Bob Kahn, who with Vint Cerf published the 1974 paper that defined TCP/IP.
kahn.section_title: Four nodes. A Cold War. The internet's first heartbeat.

kernel.definition: The one program that always runs and owns the hardware, forcing every other program to ask its permission; it shares the machine between programs and protects them from each other.
kernel.section_title: Why the kernel had to be invented

kleinrock.definition: Leonard Kleinrock, whose 1962 MIT thesis gave packet networks their queueing mathematics, and whose UCLA lab sent ARPANET's first message in 1969.
kleinrock.section_title: Four nodes. A Cold War. The internet's first heartbeat.

kubernetes.definition: The container orchestrator built at Google, descended from its internal Borg and open-sourced in 2014, that runs fleets of containers through reconcile loops over a declared desired state.
kubernetes.section_title: The orchestrator that took over deployment.

kvm.definition: A type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor, like ESXi, Xen and Hyper-V, of the kind every public cloud uses.
kvm.section_title: One physical machine · pretending to be many.

leader election.definition: The first phase of Raft: nodes wait out randomised timeouts, and the first to expire starts a new term, requests votes and, with a majority, becomes leader.
leader election.section_title: Many machines · agreement · the math says it shouldn't quite work · we make it work anyway.

least privilege.definition: The discipline that every component runs with the minimum permissions it needs, so a successful exploit of one component cannot compromise everything around it.
least privilege.section_title: The same problem from the other side · what does the attacker control?

little s law.definition: L = λ · W: the average number of items in a stable queueing system equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in it.

livelock.definition: The spinning cousin of deadlock: threads keep retrying and failing instead of blocking, so the program looks busy while making no progress.
livelock.section_title: Two threads · one variable · everything depends on luck.

liveness.definition: The guarantee that a protocol always eventually reaches a decision; FLP shows that no deterministic consensus protocol can promise it alongside safety under pure asynchrony.
liveness.section_title: Many machines · agreement · the math says it shouldn't quite work · we make it work anyway.

loadable kernel modules.definition: Drivers and filesystems compiled separately from the Linux kernel and loaded or unloaded at runtime (insmod, rmmod); they still run in Ring 0.
loadable kernel modules.section_title: The kernel is just a program

lock ordering.definition: The standard deadlock prevention: every thread acquires locks in the same global order, so the wait-for graph can never form a cycle.
lock ordering.section_title: Two threads · one variable · everything depends on luck.

lock-free.definition: Describes concurrent data structures built on compare-and-swap instead of locks, in which the system as a whole always makes progress even if individual threads starve.
lock-free.section_title: Concurrency without locks · the deeper rabbit hole.

log replication.definition: The second phase of Raft: the leader appends client commands to its log, sends them to followers, and commits each entry once a majority acknowledge it.
log replication.section_title: Many machines · agreement · the math says it shouldn't quite work · we make it work anyway.

logic gate.definition: A small circuit of a few transistors that takes one or two input bits and produces one output bit according to a Boolean rule.

mac address.definition: A 48-bit identifier burned into a network card at manufacture, identifying a device on the local link; its first 24 bits name the manufacturer.

macrotask queue.definition: The queue, also called the callback queue, of JavaScript callbacks ready to run from completed I/O, expired timers and DOM events; the event loop takes one per turn.
macrotask queue.section_title: One thread. Never blocking. Forever in motion.

malloc.definition: C's function that asks the allocator for n bytes of heap and returns their address; free hands them back.
malloc.section_title: You allocated it. You free it.

man-in-the-middle.definition: An attack in which an adversary positioned between client and server relays each side's traffic to the other, reading or rewriting it in flight.
man-in-the-middle.section_title: Where the network can lie · and where TLS prevents it from mattering.

manchester encoding.definition: A line code that puts a transition in the middle of every bit, embedding the clock in the data at the cost of double bandwidth; used by 10 Mbps Ethernet.
manchester encoding.section_title: How a one-or-zero rides on a continuous wave.

mantissa.definition: The field of a floating-point number that holds its significant digits; in an IEEE 754 double it is 52 bits, giving about 15 to 17 decimal digits of precision.

memory hierarchy.definition: The tiers of storage, from registers and caches through RAM to disk, that grow larger, slower and cheaper the further they sit from the CPU.

memory management unit.definition: The hardware unit built into the CPU that translates every virtual address to a physical one on each load and store, using the kernel's page tables.

memory ordering.definition: A contract attached to each atomic operation about what other cores are guaranteed to see, ranging from relaxed up to sequentially consistent.
memory ordering.section_title: Concurrency without locks · the deeper rabbit hole.

memory-mapped i o.definition: The channel in which device registers sit at fixed physical addresses, so the CPU talks to a device by ordinary loads and stores to those addresses.
memory-mapped i o.section_title: How the CPU reaches beyond itself

memory-safe.definition: Describes a language, such as Rust, Java, Python or Go, whose runtime or compiler checks every array access against the array's real length before the write lands.
memory-safe.section_title: The bug that defined three decades of security

merkle trees.definition: Trees of hashes in which each non-leaf node is the hash of its children's hashes, allowing compact proofs that a leaf belongs; Certificate Transparency's logs are built on them.
merkle trees.section_title: The fingerprint that does not let you reconstruct the face.

mesi.definition: The hardware cache-coherence protocol that marks every cache line on every core Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid, so no two cores hold conflicting writes to one line.
mesi.section_label: 06 · NUMA & MESI · the modern hardware reality
mesi.section_title: Memory is not flat any more · cache coherence is the only reason it pretends to be.

metcalfe.definition: Bob Metcalfe, who invented Ethernet at Xerox PARC in 1973, carrying onto a wire the ALOHAnet radio idea whose mathematics had rescued his rejected doctoral thesis.

microkernel.definition: A kernel that keeps only the minimum in Ring 0 (message passing, basic memory protection, minimal scheduling) and runs drivers and filesystems as user-space processes.
microkernel.section_title: The kernel is just a program

microservices.definition: An architecture that splits one application into many small services, each owning its own data and talking over the network, so function calls become network calls.
microservices.section_title: Architecture is fashion · the same problems return every fifteen years.

mitm.definition: Man-in-the-middle: an attack in which an adversary between two parties relays their traffic while reading or rewriting it; TLS reduces it to denial of service.
mitm.section_label: 06 · Putting it together · TLS at depth · post-quantum
mitm.section_title: Where every primitive lands · and what threatens them.

mitnick.definition: Kevin Mitnick, who on Christmas Day 1994 used IP spoofing and sequence-number prediction to break into Tsutomu Shimomura's network, and was arrested in February 1995.
mitnick.section_label: 06 · SYN floods, cookies, and the rest

ml-dsa.definition: The lattice-based post-quantum signature standard, formerly Dilithium, published by NIST in August 2024 to replace RSA and ECDSA signatures.
ml-dsa.section_label: 06 · Putting it together · TLS at depth · post-quantum
ml-dsa.section_title: Where every primitive lands · and what threatens them.

ml-kem.definition: The lattice-based post-quantum key-exchange standard, formerly Kyber, published by NIST in August 2024 to replace RSA and ECDH key exchange.
ml-kem.section_label: 06 · Putting it together · TLS at depth · post-quantum
ml-kem.section_title: Where every primitive lands · and what threatens them.

mmap.definition: The system call that maps a file into a process's address space, so each page is read from disk only when first touched, through a page fault.

mmio.definition: Memory-mapped I/O: device registers placed at fixed physical addresses, so the kernel talks to a device with ordinary loads and stores to those addresses.
mmio.section_title: How the CPU reaches beyond itself

mmu.definition: Memory management unit: the circuit between the CPU and RAM that translates every virtual address to a physical one, checks permissions and raises a page fault when something is wrong.
mmu.section_title: The hardware that draws the walls between processes

modulation.definition: Varying a property of a carrier wave (amplitude, frequency or phase) in step with the data, so bits can ride on a medium that cannot carry them directly.
modulation.section_title: How a one-or-zero rides on a continuous wave.

monolithic kernel.definition: A kernel that runs everything in Ring 0 (scheduling, memory management, filesystems, drivers, network stacks): fast, but one bug can compromise the whole machine.
monolithic kernel.section_title: The kernel is just a program

moore s law is ending.definition: Moore's Law, the doubling of transistor density roughly every two years, has slowed to a near-halt below 3 nanometres, where transistors are a few atoms wide.
moore s law is ending.section_title: The substrate is changing again · which parts will survive it?

mosfet.definition: Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor: the modern transistor, in which a gate's electric field reaches across an insulating oxide to open a conducting channel between source and drain.

move semantics.definition: The C++11 mechanism that lets one object take over another's internal buffers instead of copying them, leaving the source valid but empty.

mss.definition: Maximum Segment Size: the largest amount of data a TCP endpoint accepts in one segment; a SYN cookie spends a few bits remembering the client's MSS.
mss.section_label: 06 · SYN floods, cookies, and the rest

mtu.definition: Maximum transmission unit: the largest packet a link can carry in one piece (1500 bytes on standard Ethernet); anything larger must be fragmented.

multi-level page table.definition: A page table built as a tree (four levels on x86-64), so a sparse 48-bit address space needs a few megabytes of tables instead of 512 GB.

multics.definition: The vast time-sharing operating system, meant as a computing utility, that Bell Labs helped build until pulling out in 1969; Thompson and Ritchie, former contributors, went on to build UNIX.
multics.section_label: 02 · Ritchie and Thompson at Bell Labs
multics.section_title: Two men, a discarded minicomputer, four years.

multisets.definition: Collections, also called bags, that may hold duplicates; SQL works on multisets, keeping duplicate rows unless SELECT DISTINCT is written, where relational algebra uses sets.
multisets.section_title: The math under SQL · three operators do most of the work.

mutex.definition: A mutual exclusion lock: only one thread can hold it at a time, so the critical section it guards runs serially while other callers block.
mutex.section_title: Two threads · one variable · everything depends on luck.

mvcc.definition: Multi-version concurrency control: writers append new row versions stamped with a transaction id and each reader sees a snapshot, so readers and writers never block each other.
mvcc.section_title: The four properties that make money safe to move.

namespace.definition: A Linux kernel feature that gives a process its own view of a resource (process IDs, network, mounts, users, hostname and more); with cgroups, the basis of containers.

nan.definition: Not a Number: the IEEE 754 special value for an operation with no meaningful answer, such as 0.0 / 0.0; it spreads through later arithmetic and equals nothing, even itself.

nand.definition: NOT-AND: a gate that outputs 0 only when both inputs are 1; it is a universal gate, since NOT, AND and OR can all be built from NANDs alone.

nat.definition: Network Address Translation: rewriting addresses at a translation layer so many machines share one public IPv4 address; CGNAT is the ISP-scale version.
nat.section_title: The thirty-year migration that still isn't done.

navigational.definition: Codd's name for pre-relational databases such as IMS and CODASYL, whose programs walked pointer to pointer through tree- or network-shaped data.
navigational.section_title: One paper. One change of model. Fifty years of consequence.

node js.definition: The runtime Ryan Dahl built in 2009 by taking V8 out of the browser and adding an asynchronous I/O layer, carrying the browser's event loop to the server.
node js.section_title: An interpreter that pretended to be a compiler · then a runtime that escaped the browser.

nor.definition: NOT-OR: a gate that outputs 1 only when both inputs are 0, an OR with its output inverted.

nrz.definition: Non-Return to Zero: the simplest line code, high voltage for 1 and low for 0, which loses synchronisation on long runs of identical bits.
nrz.section_title: How a one-or-zero rides on a continuous wave.

numa.definition: Non-Uniform Memory Access: on a multi-socket machine each socket has its own local memory, and a thread reaching another socket's memory pays a 50–100% latency penalty.
numa.section_label: 06 · NUMA & MESI · the modern hardware reality
numa.section_title: Memory is not flat any more · cache coherence is the only reason it pretends to be.

number theory.definition: The mathematics of the integers, on which the cryptography of Chapter 14, and so TLS, rests; one of the primitives that outlast every substrate.
number theory.section_title: The substrate is changing again · which parts will survive it?

nx.definition: No-eXecute: the page-table bit, added to x86 by AMD in 2003, that marks a page non-executable so the MMU refuses to run instructions from it.
nx.section_title: The arms race the OS fought back

on distributed communications.definition: Paul Baran's eleven RAND memoranda, arguing for a richly connected mesh network with no central authority, routing message blocks independently so it could survive a nuclear strike.
on distributed communications.section_title: Four nodes. A Cold War. The internet's first heartbeat.

one-way function.definition: A computation that is easy to run forward and infeasible to run backward; every primitive in modern cryptography is built on one.
one-way function.section_title: Three ideas before the algorithms · so the rest of the chapter is grounded.

opcode.definition: The part of a machine instruction that says which operation to perform; in x86 the opcode byte can also encode which register the operation uses.

orms.definition: Object-relational mappers, such as Django ORM and ActiveRecord: libraries that map program objects to database rows and parameterise queries by default.
orms.section_title: String concatenation as the attack vector that will not die.

osi model.definition: The seven-layer reference model (Physical up to Application) standardised by ISO in 1984: the teaching reference, while TCP/IP's four layers run the internet.
osi model.section_title: Why every textbook draws the same cake.

oui.definition: Organizationally Unique Identifier: the first 24 bits of a MAC address, assigned by the IEEE to the manufacturer, so the address tells you who built the card.

out-of-order execution.definition: Running a later instruction before an earlier one when it does not depend on that result, so the CPU keeps working while the earlier one waits for memory.

p vs np.definition: The most famous open problem in computer science: whether every problem whose answer is quick to check is also quick to solve; if P=NP, modern cryptography largely collapses.
p vs np.section_title: Three ideas before the algorithms · so the rest of the chapter is grounded.

pac.definition: Pointer Authentication Code: ARM's hardware defence that cryptographically signs return addresses, making forgery infeasible; one response to return-oriented programming.
pac.section_title: The arms race the OS fought back

packet switching.definition: Chopping messages into small chunks, each labelled with its destination and routed independently through a shared network, the receiver reassembling them: the architecture of ARPANET and the internet.

page fault.definition: The hardware exception the MMU raises when a virtual page has no valid mapping; the kernel's handler then maps it, fetches it from disk, or sends the process SIGSEGV.

page table.definition: The kernel-maintained table that maps a process's virtual pages to physical page frames in RAM, which the MMU consults to translate addresses.

pages.definition: The fixed-size blocks, typically 4 KB, into which memory is divided: virtual pages in a process's address space, physical pages (page frames) in RAM.

parameterised queries.definition: Queries, also called prepared statements, whose SQL text and data values reach the database separately, so input is never parsed as code; the fix for SQL injection.
parameterised queries.section_title: String concatenation as the attack vector that will not die.

parc.definition: Xerox PARC, the research lab where in 1973 Bob Metcalfe invented Ethernet while Alan Kay's group worked on the Alto personal computer and Gary Starkweather on the laser printer.

partial synchrony.definition: The assumption that messages eventually arrive within some bound; Paxos and Raft rely on it to escape FLP, so they may pause but never decide wrong.
partial synchrony.section_title: Many machines · agreement · the math says it shouldn't quite work · we make it work anyway.

partition tolerance.definition: In the CAP theorem, the property that the system keeps working when the network splits the cluster; since partitions happen anyway, the real choice is consistency or availability.
partition tolerance.section_title: Pick two · the unavoidable trade in distributed storage.

paxos.definition: Leslie Lamport's classic consensus protocol (1989): two-phase prepare and accept rounds whose overlapping majorities ensure a chosen value is never lost; correct, but notoriously hard to reason about.
paxos.section_title: Many machines · agreement · the math says it shouldn't quite work · we make it work anyway.

per-stream multiplexing.definition: A QUIC feature: each stream is ordered independently, so a lost packet in one HTTP request no longer blocks the others, curing HTTP/2-over-TCP head-of-line blocking.
per-stream multiplexing.section_title: Three answers to TCP's mid-life crisis.

pgp.definition: Pretty Good Privacy: the usable email encryption program built on RSA that Phil Zimmermann released on the internet in June 1991.
pgp.section_title: Two thousand years of trying to keep secrets · and the 1976 paper that changed everything.

phil zimmermann.definition: Phil Zimmermann, the Boulder software engineer who wrote PGP in 1991 and faced a three-year US criminal export investigation, dropped in 1996.
phil zimmermann.section_title: Two thousand years of trying to keep secrets · and the 1976 paper that changed everything.

picoctf.definition: Carnegie Mellon's free, continuously running teaching CTF; the canonical first stop for learning security.
picoctf.section_label: 06 · The culture · the ecosystem of breaking and fixing
picoctf.section_title: The unified theory · and the people who keep the system honest.

pipe.definition: A kernel-allocated ring buffer with two file descriptors, one for writing and one for reading: a one-way byte stream between processes, written | in the shell.

pipeline.definition: A shell chain of processes joined by pipes, each reading standard input and writing standard output, as in cat server.log | grep "^ERROR" | sort | wc -l.

pipelining.definition: Overlapping the stages of different instructions, like an assembly line, so that while one executes the next is decoded and the one after is fetched.

pointer.definition: A variable holding a memory address, which the compiler labels with the type of thing it points at; in C, an integer address.
pointer.section_title: A pointer is an integer with attitude.

pointer arithmetic.definition: Adding to a pointer in units of the pointed-to type, not bytes: if p is an int *, p + 1 advances by sizeof(int), four bytes on most systems.
pointer arithmetic.section_title: A pointer is an integer with attitude.

polymorphism.definition: One call site reaching different implementations according to the object's actual type; in C++, a call through a slot in the object's vtable.

post-quantum cryptography.definition: Public-key systems built on lattice problems or hash functions, not factoring or discrete logarithms, so quantum computers should not break them; NIST published the first standards in 2024.
post-quantum cryptography.section_label: 06 · Putting it together · TLS at depth · post-quantum
post-quantum cryptography.section_title: Where every primitive lands · and what threatens them.

preemptive.definition: Of multitasking: the kernel forcibly takes the CPU back from a running process at regular intervals, driven by the timer interrupt.

preimage resistance.definition: The property of a cryptographic hash that, given a hash, you cannot practically find any input that produces it.
preimage resistance.section_title: The mathematics that makes the rest of the chapter possible.

privilege escalation.definition: An attack in which a process gains more privilege than it was supposed to have, either vertically (up the ladder) or horizontally (into a peer's data).

privilege ring.definition: One of the CPU's hardware privilege levels; operating systems use two, Ring 0 for the kernel, which may run any instruction, and Ring 3 for user programs, which cannot.

process.definition: A running program together with the private virtual address space the kernel gives it, kept apart from other processes by the MMU's page tables.
process.section_title: The hardware that draws the walls between processes

promise.definition: In Paxos, an acceptor's reply to a prepare message: a pledge not to accept any lower-numbered proposal, returning whatever value it has already accepted.
promise.section_title: Many machines · agreement · the math says it shouldn't quite work · we make it work anyway.

promises.definition: JavaScript objects representing a future value, standardised in ES6 (2015), with .then() and .catch() chained instead of callbacks nested: the second era of asynchronous code.
promises.section_title: One thread. Never blocking. Forever in motion.

pwn.definition: Hacker slang for taking over a system, and the CTF category of binary exploitation, such as the buffer overflows of Chapter 3.
pwn.section_label: 06 · The culture · the ecosystem of breaking and fixing
pwn.section_title: The unified theory · and the people who keep the system honest.

pwn2own.definition: A contest where researchers break shipping products live on stage; Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative funds the prizes, buys the exploits and reports them to the vendors.
pwn2own.section_label: 06 · The culture · the ecosystem of breaking and fixing
pwn2own.section_title: The unified theory · and the people who keep the system honest.

queueing theory.definition: The mathematics of waiting lines, developed in the early 20th century by Agner Krarup Erlang for telephone networks and underlying scheduling.

quic.definition: Quick UDP Internet Connections: Google's transport protocol (from around 2012, IETF standard 2021) that replaces TCP, building reliability, encryption and multiplexing over UDP in user space.
quic.section_title: Three answers to TCP's mid-life crisis.

quorum.definition: The smallest set of nodes whose agreement counts as the cluster's decision, ⌊N/2⌋ + 1; any two quorums share a node, which is what prevents split brain.
quorum.section_title: Many machines · agreement · the math says it shouldn't quite work · we make it work anyway.

race condition.definition: A bug whose outcome depends on how threads' operations interleave, as when two unsynchronised counter++ updates overlap and one increment vanishes.
race condition.section_title: Two threads · one variable · everything depends on luck.

raft.definition: Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout's consensus protocol (2014), designed to be more understandable than Paxos, with one leader, sequential terms and an explicit log; etcd runs it.
raft.section_title: Many machines · agreement · the math says it shouldn't quite work · we make it work anyway.
